ASSIGNMENT 1

Fundamentals of Immunology and Immunochemistry

________________________________________

Course Code: MCB 307
Assignment: Assignment 1
Student Name: ________________________
Matriculation Number: ________________________
Department: Microbiology
Date: ________________________

Due: Wednesday

Question 1: Immunology, Immunochemistry and Their Relationship

1.1 Definition of Immunology

Immunology is the branch of biomedical science that studies the immune system — its structure, development, function and regulation — together with the host's defence mechanisms against infectious agents and the consequences of those mechanisms. It examines how the body distinguishes "self" from "non-self", how it responds to pathogens, and what happens when these responses are excessive, deficient or misdirected. Its scope therefore extends well beyond infection to include allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, transplantation, tumour immunity and vaccination.

1.2 Definition of Immunochemistry

Immunochemistry is the sub-discipline that studies the chemical and molecular basis of immune phenomena. It deals with the structure, properties and interactions of the molecules of immunity — principally antigens and antibodies — including the chemical nature of antigen–antibody binding, antibody specificity and affinity, the structure of immunoglobulins, and the complement system. It also covers the use of antibodies as analytical reagents in techniques such as ELISA, immunodiffusion, immunoelectrophoresis, Western blotting and flow cytometry.

1.3 The Relationship Between Immunology and Immunochemistry

The two fields are closely related but operate at different levels of enquiry. Immunology is the broader biological discipline that asks how the body defends itself and how the immune system behaves as a whole; immunochemistry is the molecular and chemical arm of that discipline, asking which molecules are involved and how they interact chemically. Their relationship can be summarised as follows:

Foundation: Immunochemistry supplies the molecular explanation for immunological observations. The specificity of an immune response, for example, is explained chemically by the complementary fit between an antibody's antigen-binding site and an epitope on the antigen.

Tool: Immunological questions (e.g. "is this patient immune to a virus?") are frequently answered using immunochemical methods (e.g. ELISA, agglutination, immunoblotting).

Mutual dependence: Advances in one drive the other — understanding antibody structure (immunochemistry) enabled the design of vaccines and diagnostic tests (immunology), while immunological discoveries generate new molecular targets for chemical study.

In short, immunology provides the biological framework and immunochemistry provides the molecular detail and analytical techniques; together they form a single, integrated field of study.

Question 2: Contributions of Five Pioneers of Immunology

The table below summarises the key contribution of each scientist, the problem it helped address, and its relevance to modern immunology.

Scientist

	

Contribution

	

Problem It Helped Address

	

Relevance to Modern Immunology




Edward Jenner
(1749–1823)

	

Developed the first vaccine (1796) by inoculating a boy with cowpox material to protect against smallpox; introduced the term "vaccination".

	

Smallpox was a highly contagious, often fatal disease with no reliable protection; variolation was risky.

	

Established the principle of vaccination and immunological memory — the foundation of all modern vaccine programmes; regarded as the "father of immunology".




Louis Pasteur
(1822–1895)

	

Developed vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies using attenuated (weakened) pathogens; advanced the germ theory of disease.

	

Infectious diseases caused widespread death; there was no systematic way to induce protective immunity safely.

	

Introduced the principle of attenuation and the germ theory, providing the scientific basis for vaccine development and the microbial cause of disease.




Élie Metchnikoff
(1845–1916)

	

Discovered phagocytosis (1882) — the engulfment of microbes by phagocytic cells (macrophages and neutrophils); founded cellular immunity.

	

It was unclear how the body actually eliminates invading microorganisms at the cellular level.

	

Laid the foundation of cellular immunology and innate immunity; shared the 1908 Nobel Prize with Ehrlich.




Paul Ehrlich
(1854–1915)

	

Proposed the side-chain (receptor) theory of antibody formation; coined the term "antibody"; founded humoral immunity; also pioneered staining and chemotherapy (Salvarsan).

	

The specificity of the immune response and how antibodies neutralise toxins were unexplained.

	

Established the concepts of antigen–antibody specificity and cell receptors, underpinning humoral immunity, serology and modern immunopharmacology; shared the 1908 Nobel Prize.




Karl Landsteiner
(1868–1943)

	

Discovered the ABO blood groups (1901) and, with Wiener, the Rh factor (1940); developed the basis of blood typing.

	

Blood transfusions frequently caused fatal reactions because donor and recipient blood were incompatible.

	

Founded immunohematology and made safe blood transfusion possible; central to transplantation immunology and the study of alloimmunity; Nobel Prize 1930.

Together these pioneers illustrate the two arms of immunity — the cellular (Metchnikoff) and the humoral (Ehrlich) — and the practical translation of immunology into vaccination (Jenner, Pasteur) and clinical immunohematology (Landsteiner).

Question 3: Evaluating the Claim That Immunology Is Only the Study of How the Body Fights Microorganisms

3.1 The Claim

A student claims: "Immunology is only the study of how the body fights microorganisms."

3.2 Evaluation

The statement is an oversimplification and is therefore inaccurate. While defence against microorganisms is an important part of immunology, it is not the whole of it. Immunology also studies immune responses directed at harmless substances, at the body's own tissues, and at non-microbial foreign material such as transplanted organs and tumour cells. Two examples outside infectious disease demonstrate this clearly.

Example 1: Autoimmunity

In autoimmune diseases the immune system mounts a response against the body's own molecules rather than against a microorganism. In Type 1 diabetes, autoreactive T cells and antibodies destroy the insulin-producing β-cells of the pancreas; in rheumatoid arthritis the immune system attacks the synovial lining of joints; in multiple sclerosis it attacks the myelin sheath of nerve cells. No microorganism is being fought — the target is "self". Immunology must therefore explain self–non-self discrimination and the breakdown of immune tolerance, which lie outside the study of host–microbe conflict.
